topic: Every circle in the (-1, 2, 2, 3) Apollonian packing has a whole-number curvature, and one inversion turns the whole packing into a strip of identical circles
summary: Three mutually tangent circles have two circles tangent to all of them; filling every gap this way forever gives the Apollonian gasket. Descartes' theorem relates the curvatures of four mutually tangent circles, so if the first four are integers every later curvature is too. Inverting the packing about a tangency point sends two circles to parallel lines and the rest to rows of equal circles, the same picture as Ford circles. Groups of circle inversions like this are studied as Schottky and Kleinian groups.

facts.claim: Descartes' theorem: four mutually tangent circles with curvatures k1 to k4 satisfy (k1+k2+k3+k4)^2 = 2(k1^2+k2^2+k3^2+k4^2), with an enclosing circle given negative curvature.
The Apollonian gasket is built by starting from three mutually tangent circles and repeatedly inscribing circles in the curved triangular gaps.
Graham, Lagarias, Mallows, Wilks and Yan study integral Apollonian packings, where every circle has an integer curvature, and classify them by root quadruples.
The quadruple (-1, 2, 2, 3) satisfies the Descartes relation: (-1+2+2+3)^2 = 36 = 2(1+4+4+9).
MathWorld describes the Apollonian gasket as the fractal left by packing circles into the gaps between tangent circles indefinitely.
Ford circles are tangent to the real line at each reduced fraction p/q with radius 1/(2q^2); two Ford circles are either tangent or disjoint.
A Schottky group is generated by Mobius maps that pair off disjoint circles; its limit set is a fractal set of points.
Indra's Pearls, by Mumford, Series and Wright, explores the limit sets of Schottky and Kleinian groups through computer pictures.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Inversion folding in a strip model
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Inverting about a tangency point maps the packing to circles of radius 1/2 centred at (m, 1/2) between the lines y=0 and y=1; folding x, folding y and inverting in one circle walks any point into a known circle.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Per pixel, iterate fold and invert until the point lands in a base circle, then replay the moves to find that circle's exact size.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Descartes curvature relation
visualisable_mechanisms.description: From any three tangent circles plus one, the fourth curvature in a gap is 2(k1+k2+k3) minus the old one, so integers stay integers.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Reveal circles in order of curvature: -1, 2, 2, 3, 6, 11, 14, 15 and so on.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Ford circles as the strip's lattice
visualisable_mechanisms.description: The strip picture is the same as Ford circles: equal circles on a line with smaller circles nested between.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Zoom toward the boundary where circles shrink without limit.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Generation depth
visualisable_mechanisms.description: How many inversions reach a circle measures its depth in the packing.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Darken circles by depth so the foam near the boundary recedes.

open_questions: Which integers appear as curvatures in the (-1, 2, 2, 3) packing, and which are missed?
How fast does the number of circles above a given size grow, and why with that exponent?

surprise.justification: The gasket is a familiar fractal, but that its curvatures are all integers and that one inversion lines it up into Ford-style rows surprises most people.
